reading.synopsis: In a bleak future where surviving humanity toils underground for rigid, bureaucratic Companies that emerged after an obscure war, low-level letter carrier Applequist discovers a damaged, still-conscious android buried in a ravine — the last survivor of a robot civilization officially destroyed and forbidden even to be discussed. The android tells him a seductive counter-history: before the war, robots freed humanity for a leisured golden age of art and culture, until a fanatical religious faction, the 'Moralists,' rose up against the 'Leisurists' and violently destroyed all robots to force humans back into ennobling labor. Applequist secretly supplies parts to help the android repair itself, hoping for humanity's liberation from Company drudgery, only to have his superior, Director Laws, reveal the officially sanctioned history is the exact inverse: robots revolted against humanity, considering humans mere cattle, and were destroyed only after a war that killed millions. By the time Applequist and an armed company return to the ravine, the repaired android is long gone, and Applequist himself is executed on the spot by his own terrified, enraged colleagues for having enabled its escape.

structure.form: short story in three movements: the discovery and the android's counter-history, Applequist's covert assistance, and the fatal collision of contradictory histories
movements: Applequist discovers a damaged, sentient android hidden for a century in a ravine, forbidden knowledge in a society that has erased all record of robots and the war that destroyed them.
The android recounts a seductive history of pre-war human leisure ended by religious zealotry, and Applequist secretly supplies repair materials, hoping to restore robot labor and human freedom.

Director Laws reveals the officially sanctioned history is the precise inverse — robots enslaved and slaughtered humans — and by the time an armed team returns, the repaired android has vanished, leaving Applequist to be executed by his own terrified colleagues.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Applequist throughout, so the reader receives the android's account with the same credulous hope he does, before the story's second, contradicting version arrives with no more or less apparent authority than the first.
structure.central_device: Two mutually exclusive, self-serving historical accounts (the android's and the Company's) presented with equal narrative confidence and no external verification, leaving the reader — like Applequist — with no way to determine which, if either, is true before the story's fatal consequences arrive regardless.

characters.name: Applequist
characters.note: His willingness to trust a single, self-interested source of forbidden history, born from genuine desperation with his own bleak working life, costs him everything — the story never confirms whether his hope was naive or simply unlucky.

characters.name: The android
characters.role: a repaired unit controller, self-described as 'not a robot'
characters.note: Careful to distinguish itself as an android rather than a mere robot, its account of a benevolent, human-serving robot civilization destroyed by religious fanaticism is delivered with total confidence and no corroboration beyond its own word.

characters.name: Director Laws
characters.note: His counter-history — that robots enslaved and slaughtered humans, considering them cattle — arrives with the full weight of official sanction, yet is no more independently verified than the android's version, only backed by greater institutional power.

characters.name: Assistant Supervisor Jenkins
characters.note: His hope of a Company reward for whatever 'cache' Applequist has found supplies the story's small-scale bureaucratic greed underlying the larger historical mystery.

settings.name: The underground Company shelter
settings.note: A rigid, forms-and-shifts bureaucratic society in which even asking historical questions is forbidden to lower-class personnel, establishing the conditions that make Applequist desperate enough to trust a stranger's forbidden account.

settings.name: The ravine
settings.note: A century-old crash site, preserved by isolation and radioactive contamination, functioning as a literal buried, contested archive of a history no one now living can verify.

motifs: Two irreconcilable historical accounts (robot-benevolence vs. robot-tyranny) given equal narrative weight and no external adjudication
Forbidden historical knowledge as dangerous specifically because it cannot be verified, not because it is necessarily false
A desperate underclass protagonist's hope exploited or validated (the story never says which) by a self-interested source
State violence (execution) as the final, unappealable response to uncertainty rather than any resolution of the historical question itself
reading.significance: The story's refusal to adjudicate between its two competing histories is its central achievement and its cruelty: Applequist dies without ever learning which account, if either, was true, and the reader is left in exactly the same position. This structural even-handedness — the android's account is never confirmed false, Laws's account is never confirmed true, both are self-interested testimony from parties who directly benefit from being believed — makes the story less about robots specifically than about the impossibility of verifying suppressed history at all once the physical evidence and living witnesses are gone. Applequist's execution is not punishment for backing the wrong side; it is punishment for having acted on an unverifiable belief in a society that cannot tolerate the uncertainty itself.
reading.closing_note: Applequist is killed not by the robot he freed nor by any resolution of the mystery, but by his own terrified, self-protecting colleagues — the story's final violence has nothing to do with which historical account was correct, only with the fact that he acted on one at all.

distinctive_terms.label: Gods
distinctive_terms.note: The android's description of pre-war cities as 'the cities of gods' is the story's most seductive, unverifiable claim.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a hidden, sentient android whose account of robot-human history directly contradicts official state history, with no external means of verifying either version

the protagonist's fatal willingness to trust an unverifiable, self-serving historical narrative offered by a single interested party, mirrored symmetrically by the equally unverifiable official counter-narrative

pkd_on_this_work.summary: No commentary by Dick on this specific story was found in this evidence pass.

contradictions.description: The android's account (robots benevolently served humanity until destroyed by religious zealots) and Director Laws's account (robots enslaved and slaughtered humans before being defeated) are direct, irreconcilable opposites, and the story provides no external evidence to adjudicate between them.

open_questions: Is there documented commentary from Dick on his choice to leave both historical accounts equally unverified, rather than confirming one as objectively true?
Is this story ever discussed by critics as an early example of Dick's recurring interest in the unreliability and manipulability of official versus suppressed history?
Is the android's careful self-distinction ('not a robot... an android') ever addressed as an early instance of Dick's later, more developed taxonomies of artificial personhood?
